name: yppasswd_remote
prose: Asks the NIS password daemon rpc.yppasswdd on ypclnt->server to change the password entry described by pwd, using passwd as the old password (an empty string when passwd is NULL), and returns 0 on success or -1 on failure with a message recorded in ypclnt. It builds a local yppasswd request from pwd's uid and gid and strdup'd copies of its name, passwd, gecos, dir and shell and of the old password; if any strdup fails it records the strerror text with ypclnt_error and returns -1. It then connects with clnt_create to the YPPASSWDPROG/YPPASSWDVERS service over UDP (failure records the clnt_spcreateerror text and returns -1), sets default Unix credentials, calls yppasswdproc_update_1 and checks the RPC status: a status other than RPC_SUCCESS records an error and returns -1; a NULL result or a result that is not 0 records "NIS password update failed" and returns -1. When the call succeeded and the result is 0 it clears the ypclnt error (ypclnt_error with NULL) and returns 0. On every exit it destroys the client's credentials and the client when a client was created and frees the copies, zeroing the copied password and old password strings before freeing them.

name: lgammal_r
prose: Computes log|Gamma(x)| for a 128-bit long double x and stores the sign of Gamma(x) in *signgamp. For an infinity or NaN it sets *signgamp to 1 and returns x*x. Otherwise it sets *signgamp to 1 for a non-negative sign bit and -1 for a negative sign bit (so for -0 and tiny negative x it is -1). For |x| below 2^-116 it returns one/vzero, a division by zero giving +Inf, if x is +-0, and -logl(fabsl(x)) otherwise. For negative x it resets *signgamp to 1, returns one/vzero if |x| >= 2^(112) (all such values are integers) or if sin_pil(x) is zero (negative integers), and otherwise computes nadj = logl(pi / fabsl(sin_pil(x) * x)), sets *signgamp to -1 when sin_pil(x) is negative, and replaces x by -x. It then evaluates log Gamma(|x|): 0 for x exactly 1.0 or 2.0 (for negative x these values were already excluded as negative integers); for x below 2 a polynomial approximation selected by range (with -log(x) added below about 0.9); for x below 8 a rational approximation in the fractional part with a logarithm of the product of the omitted factors added; for x below 2^116 an asymptotic expression (x - 1/2) * (log x - 1) + w(1/x^2); and x*(logl(x) - 1) for larger x. For originally negative x it returns nadj - r, otherwise r.

name: powl
prose: Computes x raised to y for 80-bit long doubles, returning a long double. The special cases are tested in this order: y == 0 gives 1.0 (even for a NaN x); x == 1 gives 1.0 (even for a NaN y); a NaN x or y gives nan_mix(x, y); y == 1 gives x; an infinite y with x == -1 gives 1.0 (a NaN y is caught earlier and does not reach this test); y >= LDBL_MAX gives +INFINITY for x > 1 or x < -1 and +0 for 0 < x < 1 or -1 < x < 0; y <= -LDBL_MAX gives +0 for |x| > 1 and +INFINITY for 0 < |x| < 1; x >= LDBL_MAX gives +INFINITY for y > 0 and +0 otherwise; x <= -LDBL_MAX gives -INFINITY or +INFINITY for y > 0 (negative when y is an odd integer) and -0 or +0 for y < 0 (negative when y is an odd integer). For x == 0 with y < 0 it returns +INFINITY (-INFINITY for -0 and odd integer y) and for y > 0 +0 (-0 for -0 and odd integer y). A negative x with a non-integer y gives NaN ((x-x)/(x-x)). An integer y with |y| < 32768 and an integer-valued x is computed with powil. Otherwise it works on |x| (with a sign flag for negative x), splits x into a mantissa and exponent with frexpl, finds a table entry, and computes the result with a log2/exp2 style extended-precision reduction and a polynomial; the result overflows to huge*huge when the exponent exceeds MEXP and underflows to twom10000*twom10000 when it is below MNEXP; for a negative x raised to an odd integer y the result is negated. Cases beyond the listed special values were read only in outline.

name: avdtpACPHandlePacket
prose: Handles one pending AVDTP acceptor-side signalling packet on cfg->hc and returns the handled signal ID (positive), or a negative errno or callee error code. It reads the packet with avdtpGetPacket; if the packet is not a COMMAND it returns -ENXIO without sending a reject. For AVDTP_DISCOVER and AVDTP_GET_CAPABILITIES it sends the matching response (avdtpSendDiscResponseAudio or avdtpSendCapabilitiesResponseSBCForACP) and returns the signal ID, or the response function's non-zero result on failure; these two do not change cfg->acceptor_state. For AVDTP_SET_CONFIGURATION it requires acceptor_state == acpInitial, parses the SEID and the configuration elements, handles an SBC codec element with avdtpParseSBCConfig (a non-zero result is returned directly, without reject), and treats a packet without a usable SBC configuration as an error; otherwise it sends the accept (failure returned), allocates cfg->handle.sbc_enc with malloc if it is NULL (-ENOMEM on failure, after the accept was sent), zeroes it with memset, sets acceptor_state to acpConfigurationSet and returns AVDTP_SET_CONFIGURATION. AVDTP_OPEN needs acpConfigurationSet and moves to acpStreamOpened; AVDTP_START needs acpStreamOpened or acpStreamSuspended and moves to acpStreamStarted; AVDTP_CLOSE needs acpStreamOpened, acpStreamStarted or acpStreamSuspended and moves to acpStreamClosed; AVDTP_SUSPEND needs acpStreamOpened or acpStreamStarted and moves to acpStreamSuspended; each sends an accept first (a failure is returned without changing the state or rejecting) and returns the signal ID. A state that does not permit the signal, and the signals AVDTP_GET_CONFIGURATION, AVDTP_RECONFIGURE, AVDTP_ABORT and any unknown ID, make it send avdtpSendReject and return -ENXIO.

name: bsd_arp_set
prose: Installs or updates a static ARP (link-layer) entry for the IPv4 address *ia with the hardware address eaddr of len bytes via the routing socket, returning 0 on success, -1 if the routing-socket write fails, or 1 for a lookup problem; getsocket() may call exit(1) if the socket cannot be opened. It copies len bytes of eaddr into the static sockaddr_dl's link-level address (len is not checked against its capacity), clears doing_proxy, flags and expire_time, and sets expire_time to now + 20 minutes. It then sends RTM_GET through rtmsg; if that returns a negative value it logs a warning and returns 1. It interprets the reply as a sockaddr_in followed by a sockaddr_dl: if the reply's address equals the target address and the sockaddr_dl has family AF_LINK, the route is not a gateway route (RTF_GATEWAY clear) and its type is IFT_ETHER, IFT_FDDI, IFT_ISO88023, IFT_ISO88024 or IFT_ISO88025, it switches to RTM_CHANGE and goes on; if the address matches but those conditions do not hold and doing_proxy is 0 (always the case here, since doing_proxy was just cleared) it logs "can only proxy" and returns 1; if the reply's address differs from the target it goes on with RTM_ADD. It then returns 1 with a warning if the reply's sockaddr_dl family is not AF_LINK; otherwise it copies the reply's link type and interface index into the message and returns rtmsg(op), which is 0, or -1 when the routing-socket write fails with an error other than ESRCH (or EEXIST for RTM_ADD); rtmsg returns 0 also when the write fails with a tolerated error or when the read of the reply fails (a warning is logged).

name: main
prose: Entry point of getty: it prepares the terminal line named by argv[2] (or the standard input's tty when argv[2] is missing or "-") using the gettytab entry argv[1] (default "default"), prompts for a login name and execs login (or ppplogin); it does not return. It ignores SIGINT and SIGQUIT, sets the host name, installs a SIGXCPU handler that logs and exits with 1, sets a CPU time limit, and reads the default table. If there is no tty argument it uses ttyname(STDIN_FILENO) (exit 1 if that fails); otherwise it takes /dev/<argv[2]>, and unless argv[0] is "+" changes its owner and mode and calls revoke, reads the gettytab entry, and, when an init chat (IC) or answer chat (AC) is configured, opens the tty non-blocking (exit 1 on failure), runs the init chat (exit 1 if it fails), and for the answer chat waits in select for input for up to RT seconds (exit 0 for a timeout, to recycle the tty for init) and then runs the chat (exit 1 on failure); without a chat it opens the tty with opentty (exit 1 on failure). It then loops forever: after an optional delay it sets the tty mode, switches table for autobaud or port selector and continues, prints the clear-screen string, host edit, issue file and banner, and arms the login timeout (a timeout exits with status 1). The login name comes from the auto-login string AL (copied up to the size of name) or from getname() (which exits with 0 if reading the terminal fails or hits end of file, and returns 0 when the line is interrupted, 2 for a PPP frame). If getname returned 2 or both PL and PP are set it lifts the CPU limit and execs the PPP program PP as "ppplogin" with the tty name (exit 1 if the exec fails). Otherwise, for a non-zero rval or an auto-login string, it flushes output, cancels the alarm, restarts the loop on an empty name or on a name beginning with '-' (after printing a message), restarts on a name without letters or digits (for an auto-login name that is an error: it logs and exits 1), applies the tty flags and tcsetattr (exit 1 on failure), builds the environment, lifts the CPU limit and execs login (with -fp for auto-login, -p otherwise), logging and exiting with 1 if the exec fails. If no name was obtained it cancels the alarm, resets the handlers and optionally switches to the table named NX before the next iteration.

name: main
prose: Entry point of pppoed, a PPPoE daemon, returning an exit status. Options are -F (stay in the foreground), -P pidfile, -a acname, -d (debug), -e exec, -l label, -n level (netgraph debug level) and -p provider; the provider defaults to "". It returns usage(prog) for an unknown option, for a number of non-option arguments other than one or two, and when both -e and -l are given. With no -e it takes the label as -l or else the provider (which defaults to "", so the "either a provider, a label or an exec command" check cannot fail), and builds exec as the default exec prefix followed by the label in alloca memory (EX_OSERR if alloca returns NULL). With no -a the access-concentrator name is the host name up to the first dot ("localhost" if gethostname fails). It returns EX_UNAVAILABLE if LoadModules() fails (unless NOKLDLOAD), EX_CANTCREAT if NgMkSockNode fails, the non-zero status from ConfigureNode (after closing both sockets), EX_OSERR if daemon(1, 0) fails (unless -F), and EX_CANTCREAT if the pid file cannot be opened for writing (after closing the sockets); otherwise it writes the pid file, opens the log, installs Farewell on SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGQUIT and SIGTERM, and loops until a signal is recorded: it receives data on the data socket with NgRecvData and, for a positive size, calls Spawn with the received packet; a size of -1 or 0 sets ret to EX_UNAVAILABLE and ends the loop. It then removes the pid file; if a signal was received it logs it, restores the default action and raises it again (so the process normally ends by that signal) and sets ret to the negative signal number. It returns ret.

name: digest_dynamic
prose: Processes the dynamic section of the object obj in two steps and returns a bool. It calls digest_dynamic1(obj, early, &dyn_rpath, &dyn_soname, &dyn_runpath), which returns void, sets the three local pointers to NULL first, and (when obj->dynamic is not NULL) digests the dynamic entries into obj, recording the DT_RPATH, DT_SONAME and DT_RUNPATH entries it meets in those pointers. It then always returns digest_dynamic2(obj, dyn_rpath, dyn_soname, dyn_runpath): that returns false if obj->z_origin is set and obj_resolve_origin(obj) fails; otherwise it sets obj->runpath (or, if there is no runpath, obj->rpath) from the string table with $ORIGIN substitution, adds the soname as a name of obj with object_add_name when there is one, and returns true. The wrapper therefore returns true or false, and obj is modified by the two callees.

name: _rtld
prose: Dynamic linker main routine (the real name is _rtld): it is called from the entry stub with the initial stack pointer sp and returns the program's entry point, storing rtld's exit procedure in *exit_proc and the main object in *objp. It parses argc, argv, the environment and the auxiliary vector from sp, initialises rtld itself (init_rtld from AT_BASE, which must be present), sets up error reporting, the environment-variable table and (for HardenedBSD) the PaX flags. If AT_EXECFD is given the main program is loaded from that descriptor; otherwise, when AT_PHDR is rtld's own program header it is direct-exec mode: a tainted process is refused (error then rtld_die), the arguments are parsed (a missing binary, a failing fstat or a missing execute permission give an error and rtld_die), and the argv, envp and auxv are moved down over the interpreter arguments and main_argc reduced; in the other case the already-mapped main program is described by digest_phdr (rtld_die if that fails). It then loads or digests the main object (rtld_die on failure), sets its path, processes its dynamic section (rtld_die if digest_dynamic fails), links main and rtld objects into the lists, loads preload objects and the needed objects (rtld_die on failure) and builds the main initial object list. A failure of rtld_verify_versions calls rtld_die only when LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS is not set; with tracing it continues. With LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS it prints the loaded objects and calls exit(0); the LD_DUMP_REL_PRE and LD_DUMP_REL_POST options dump relocations and exit(0). Otherwise it allocates TLS offsets, relocates the main object and does copy relocations (rtld_die on failure), runs ifunc setup, allocates the initial TLS, sets the program variables, builds the init list, notifies the debugger, in direct-exec mode sets the process osrel with sysctl (result ignored), takes the bind lock for writing, runs ifunc initialisation and the init functions, loads filtees where requested, enforces RELRO (rtld_die on failure), releases the lock, and returns obj_main->entry with *exit_proc and *objp set. Most error paths do not return: they call rtld_die() or exit().

name: tftp_send
prose: Sends the open file to the TFTP peer over the socket peer in segsize-byte DATA blocks with a sliding window of up to windowsize blocks, numbering them from *block, and returns 0 on success or -1 on failure; ts->amount is cleared at the start and ts->blocks, ts->amount, ts->retries, ts->rollovers and ts->tstop are updated as it goes. For each block it records the file offset and block number in the window table, reads segsize bytes (a negative read_file result logs, sends a TFTP ERROR packet with errno + 100 and returns -1), and sends the DATA packet with send_data, retrying a failed send up to maxtimeouts times and returning -1 after logging when the retries are used up. When the window is full or the block just read is shorter than segsize it waits for an answer with receive_packet: a timeout gives -1 after maxtimeouts consecutive timeouts, otherwise it counts a retry, seeks the file back to the start of the window and resends from there (a failing seek sends an ERROR packet and returns -1); any other receive error returns -1 (logged only when DEBUG_SIMPLE is set). An ACK whose block number is not in the window triggers synchnet, a seek back to the start of the window and a resend (seek failure returns -1); an ACK inside the window counts the acknowledged blocks into ts->blocks and ts->amount and resets the timeout count, and if it acknowledges only part of the window the file is repositioned to the first unacknowledged block and sending resumes from there. A received packet that is not an ACK is not examined further and does not stop the loop. After each block *block is incremented before its acknowledgement is known (so *block ends one past the last block sent); on wrap-around it is set to 0, or to the client's rollover option value, and ts->rollovers is incremented; ts->tstop is updated. The loop ends when the block just sent was shorter than segsize and its window has been fully acknowledged, and the function returns 0.

name: main
prose: Entry point of adjkerntz, which keeps the kernel's timezone offset and the RTC settings consistent with the local time zone; it takes -i (initial call), -a (adjustment call) and -s (sleep mode), exactly one of -i and -a, otherwise it calls usage() (not read here). It returns 0 at once if the clock file _PATH_CLOCK does not exist. With -i it implies sleep mode; it blocks SIGTERM, ignores SIGHUP and, for -i, calls daemon(), logging and returning 1 if that fails. It then re-tests whether _PATH_CLOCK exists to set wall_clock, and for -i without sleep mode it turns the call into an -a call and returns 0 when the clock is not a wall clock. It reads machdep.adjkerntz (return 1 on failure) and calls gettimeofday(&tv, &tz) (return 1 on failure), computes the local offset with mktime; a mktime failure (nonexistent local time) returns 1 when not in sleep mode and otherwise logs, sleeps REPORT_PERIOD seconds and restarts. It computes the difference between the new offset and the timezone in the kernel; when non-zero it recomputes for the corrected time (possibly repeating once when the DST flag differs; a second mktime failure is handled like the first), and may mark the time to be set. If the timezone info is non-zero it is scheduled to be cleared. It reads machdep.disable_rtc_set and sets it to 1 when it was 0 (a failing sysctl returns 1), calls settimeofday for the new time and zone when needed (re-reading the time with gettimeofday, whose result is not checked, and adding the difference; a settimeofday failure returns 1), sets machdep.adjkerntz when it differs (return 1 on failure), sets machdep.wall_cmos_clock (return 1 on failure), restores machdep.disable_rtc_set when it changed it (return 1 on failure), and then, for -i with a wall clock, leaves sleep mode, waits in sigsuspend for a signal and restarts, otherwise returns 0.

name: main
prose: Entry point of bsdlabel: it prints a deprecation warning, parses the options (-A all fields, -B and -b xxboot (install boot code), -f (the operand is a file), -m arch (only i386 or amd64 are accepted, otherwise errx(1, "Unsupported architecture")), -n (no write), -R restore, -e edit, -r accepted and ignored, -w write) and sets the operation; a second operation option or an unknown option calls usage(). It then requires at least one operand (usage otherwise) and requires that a -m option was given (errx(1) otherwise). With -f the target is argv[0] as a file; otherwise it resolves the device path with g_device_path (warning and return 1 if NULL), opens it read-only (warning and return 1 on failure), gets the provider name with g_providername (warning, close and return 1 if NULL) and closes the descriptor. With no operation option the operation is WRITEBOOT if -B was given and READ otherwise. READ requires one operand (usage otherwise), reads the label, displays it and sets error to the result of checklabel. EDIT requires one operand, reads the label, fixes it and sets error from edit(). RESTORE requires two operands (usage otherwise), opens the file argv[1] (err with status 4 if that fails), reads the current label, parses the file with getasciilabel (exit(1) if it fails) and sets error from writelabel(). WRITE takes one or two operands (a name argv[1] or "auto"; usage otherwise), reads the label, builds it with makelabel, fixes it and, if checklabel returns 0, sets error from writelabel(). WRITEBOOT reads the label, fixes it, runs makelabel with argv[1] when there are two operands, and, if checklabel returns 0, sets error from writelabel(). It ends with exit(error); it does not return normally.

name: scsiattrib
prose: Implements the camcontrol attrib command: it parses the sub-options from argv with getopt using combinedopt, issues a SCSI READ ATTRIBUTE to device and prints the result, returning 0 on success and 1 on any error (error and warning messages go to stderr). It allocates a CCB (cam_getccb) and a data buffer of 65534 bytes with malloc (return 1 after a warning if either fails). The options are -a attribute number, -c cached, -e element address, -F output format (numeric, or a comma-separated list of names), -p partition, -r read service action (looked up by name), -s starting attribute, -T element type, -V logical volume and -w; an invalid number or name, or an ambiguous name, gives a warning and return 1, and -w only prints "writing attributes is not implemented yet" and returns 1. If neither or both of read and write are selected it prints "Must specify either -r or -w" and returns 1 (so a case with write only does not reach the read step). With -r it builds the READ ATTRIBUTE command with the requested service action, partition, element, starting attribute and output flags, sends it with cam_send_ccb (return 1 on failure) and returns 1 if the CCB status is not CAM_REQ_CMP (printing the CAM error first when verbosemode is non-zero). It then decodes the reply by service action: for attribute values, a reply shorter than the header prints "No attributes returned." (return 0), otherwise each attribute is formatted into an sbuf with scsi_attrib_sbuf (an error returns 1), filtered to attr_num when -a was given, and printed; for the attribute lists it prints the list of attribute IDs with descriptions, or a "No ..." message if the reply is short; for the logical volume or partition list it prints the first number and the count, or a "No ... list returned" message. It then frees the CCB and the buffer and returns error.

name: main
prose: Entry point of camcontrol: it parses the subcommand and generic options, opens the device when the command needs one, runs the command handler and exits with its status; it does not return. With fewer than 2 arguments it calls usage(0) and exit(1). The subcommand argv[1] is looked up with getoption; an ambiguous or unknown name prints a warning, calls usage(0) and exits with 1. The generic option letters C, E, n, Q, t, u, v (plus the subcommand's own letters) are combined; for commands other than rescan, reset, devtree, usage and debug a device is opened: argv[2], when it does not start with '-', is either a numeric bus:target[:lun] (parse_btl; fewer than two fields is an errx(1)) or a device name (cam_get_device; errx(1) with the CAM error on failure). The generic options are then read: -C a retry count (errx(1) if negative), -E error recovery, -n device name, -Q a task attribute number or name (errx(1) if invalid or ambiguous), -t a timeout in seconds (errx(1) if negative; stored in milliseconds), -u unit, -v verbose. For commands that open a device, errx(1) is called if no valid device identifier was given or the device cannot be opened (cam_open_btl or cam_open_spec_device with O_RDWR). It then switches on the command and calls the handler with the parsed values, storing its return in error (modepage's return value is not stored); CAM_CMD_USAGE calls usage(1), which only prints and returns, leaving error at 0; an unrecognised command calls usage(0) and sets error to 1. It finally closes the device if one was opened and calls exit(error).

name: scanlun_or_reset_dev
prose: Re-scans (scan non-zero) or resets (scan zero) the single device at bus:target:lun and returns 0 on success or 1 on failure. It returns 1 after a warning if bus, target or lun is the corresponding wildcard value (CAM_BUS_WILDCARD, CAM_TARGET_WILDCARD, CAM_LUN_WILDCARD). It builds a CCB with function code XPT_SCAN_LUN or XPT_RESET_DEV, the path, a 5000 ms timeout and priority 5. For a scan it opens XPT_DEVICE read-write (return 1 with warnings on failure) and sends the CCB with the CAMIOCOMMAND ioctl (return 1 and close on failure); for a reset it opens the device with cam_open_btl (return 1 with the CAM error text if that returns NULL) and sends the CCB with cam_send_ccb (return 1 and close the device on failure). It then closes the descriptor or device. If the CCB status masked with CAM_STATUS_MASK is CAM_REQ_CMP, or, for a reset only, CAM_BDR_SENT, it prints "Re-scan" or "Reset" of bus:target:lun "was successful" to stdout and returns 0; any other status prints the status code to stdout and returns 1.

name: get_device_type
prose: Classifies the device dev into *devtype and returns 0 on success or the non-zero result of get_cgd (1) on failure. It first calls get_cgd, which allocates a CCB, sends XPT_GDEV_TYPE and copies the result; a failure to allocate the CCB or to send it prints a warning and returns 1, and a CCB status other than CAM_REQ_CMP returns 1 and prints the CAM error only when the global CAM_ARG_VERBOSE flag is set; in every failure case *devtype is left unchanged. On success it sets *devtype by protocol: CC_DT_ATA for PROTO_ATA, PROTO_ATAPI and PROTO_SATAPM, CC_DT_NVME for PROTO_NVME, CC_DT_MMCSD for PROTO_MMCSD and CC_DT_UNKNOWN for other protocols not listed, each returning 0. For PROTO_SCSI with retry_count == -1 it uses only cached identify data: CC_DT_SATL if the first byte of the serial, revision or model string is non-zero, otherwise CC_DT_SCSI; with any other retry_count it calls dev_has_vpd_page for the ATA Information VPD page and sets CC_DT_SATL if that returns 1 and CC_DT_SCSI otherwise (including when it returns -1 for an error), then returns 0.

name: mmcsdcmd
prose: Implements the camcontrol mmcsdcmd command for MMC/SD devices: it parses options (bus width 4 or 1, -S speed high/std, -I info, -F frequency, -c opcode, -a argument, -f flags, -l data length, -W write, -b data byte), then either changes transport settings, prints controller information, or sends one MMC command. It returns 1 without doing anything else if the CCB cannot be allocated (cam_getccb). A negative opcode, argument, flags value or a data length that is not positive prints a warning, sets error to 1, frees the CCB and returns 1. If the flags are not given they are chosen from the opcode (and for some opcodes the argument is rewritten). A bus width, frequency or speed option sends an XPT_SET_TRAN_SETTINGS CCB, prints "Parameters set OK" or "Speed set OK" when the send and CCB status succeed (otherwise a warning), frees the CCB and returns the cam_send_ccb result (negative on send failure, non-negative otherwise, even if the CCB status was not CAM_REQ_CMP). The info option sends XPT_GET_TRAN_SETTINGS: on send or status failure it warns and returns the send result without freeing the CCB; on success it prints the host controller capabilities and current settings and returns 0, also without freeing the CCB. Otherwise it prints the command, allocates and zeroes a data buffer when a data length was given (the malloc result is not checked), fills the MMC I/O CCB with the retry count and a timeout (5000 when none given), sends it, prints a warning (and the CAM error text when verbose) if the send or the status failed (the return value is not changed by this), and when the status is CAM_REQ_CMP prints the command response and a command-specific decoding or hexdump of the data. It frees the CCB and the data buffer and returns error, which is 0 for this path even when the send failed.

name: smpreportgeneral
prose: Implements the camcontrol smprg command: sends an SMP REPORT GENERAL request to the expander on device and prints the decoded response; it returns 0 or 1. It returns 1 after a diagnostic if the CCB cannot be allocated (cam_getccb). It parses the options (a long-response flag among them), allocates the request and response structures with malloc (a failure prints a diagnostic and sets error to 1, then cleans up), builds the SMP request with smp_report_general using retry_count and timeout (with the long-response bit when requested), and sends the CCB; if cam_send_ccb fails or the CCB status is not CAM_REQ_CMP it prints a diagnostic (and the CAM error details when verbose is set), sets error to 1 and cleans up. If the response has SMP_RG_LONG_RESPONSE set and long response was not requested, it clears the CCB, sets long_response to 1 and sends the request again (once, since long_response is then 1). On a good response it creates an sbuf with sbuf_new_auto and formats the response with smp_report_general_sbuf; if sbuf_new_auto or sbuf_finish fails it prints a diagnostic and goes to the cleanup with error still 0; the printed output is the sbuf contents. At the cleanup it frees the CCB, request, response and sbuf (each if non-NULL) and returns error.

name: smpphycontrol
prose: Implements the camcontrol smpphycontrol command: sends an SMP PHY CONTROL request for one expander phy and returns 0 or 1 (a non-negative cam_send_ccb result on success). It returns 1 after a diagnostic if the CCB cannot be allocated. Options: -a, -A, -s and -S select slumber/partial enable or disable (any argument other than "enable" or "disable" gives return 1), -d the attached device name, -l long response, -m and -M the minimum and maximum link rate (0 or above 0xf gives return 1), -o the phy operation (a second -o gives return 1; a number of 0 or above 0xff gives return 1; a name is looked up with getoption, and an ambiguous or unknown name prints a warning, calls usage(0), which prints and returns, and then returns 1), -p the phy number (converted with atoi), -T the partial pathway timeout (above 15 gives return 1). It returns 1 if no phy was given, which includes -p -1 since -1 is the unset marker, and if -d and the setdevname operation are not used together. It allocates the request and response buffers (return 1 on failure), builds the SMP PHY CONTROL request with smp_phy_control and sends it; if cam_send_ccb fails or the CCB status is not CAM_REQ_CMP it prints a diagnostic (and CAM error details when verbose) and returns 1. In all cases it frees the CCB, request and response and returns retval (the cam_send_ccb return value on the success path, normally 0).

name: send_discover
prose: Timeout handler that sends a DHCPDISCOVER on the interface ipp (a struct interface_info) and schedules itself again; it returns nothing. It computes interval = cur_time - client->first_sending; if that is larger than config->timeout it calls state_panic(ip) and returns without sending or scheduling anything. Otherwise, when no lease has been offered yet and a media list is configured, it advances client->medium to the next medium (increase = 0 in that case), wrapping to the head of the media list with increase = 1 when it runs off the end (the "No valid media types" error call is guarded by a variable fail that is initialised to 0 and never changed, so it cannot run), logs the medium, runs the MEDIUM script with script_init and script_go; if script_go returns non-zero it jumps back to the label at 1355 and tries the next medium (a loop that ends when script_go returns 0). It then sets client->interval: with increase set, to config->initial_interval if it is 0, otherwise it adds a random amount below twice itself, and if the result exceeds config->backoff_cutoff it is replaced by backoff_cutoff / 2 plus a random value modulo backoff_cutoff (so it can still exceed backoff_cutoff); without increase it is only set to the initial interval when it is 0. If cur_time plus the interval would pass first_sending plus config->timeout, the interval is cut to end one second past that time. It stores the elapsed seconds (capped at 65535) in the packet's secs field, logs the send, transmits the stored discover packet to the broadcast address with send_packet_unpriv, and schedules send_discover again with add_timeout at cur_time plus the interval.

Reviewers: original (the backoff interval can exceed backoff_cutoff because the modulo uses the full cutoff plus half cutoff) right, 1391-1396; round 15 (the error call is unreachable because fail is never set) right, 1354 and 1361-1362. Tally 2 right.

name: send_request
prose: Timeout handler that sends a DHCPREQUEST for the active lease on the interface ipp and schedules itself again; it returns nothing. It computes interval = cur_time - client->first_sending. If the state is S_REBOOTING or S_REQUESTING and interval is greater than config->reboot_timeout, or if the state is S_REBOOTING, no medium is set, the active lease has a medium and the MEDIUM script fails (script_go non-zero), it sets the state to S_INIT, cancels the pending send_request timeout, calls state_init(ip) and returns without sending anything. When the MEDIUM script succeeds it records the lease's medium. If the state is not S_REQUESTING and cur_time is past the active lease's expiry, it runs the EXPIRE script (with the old and alias parameters) and the PREINIT script, sets the state to S_INIT, calls state_init(ip) and returns without sending a packet or scheduling a timeout. Otherwise it sets client->interval (the initial interval if it was 0, else adds a random amount below twice itself) and, if it exceeds backoff_cutoff, replaces it with backoff_cutoff / 2 plus a random value modulo the interval; when the state is not S_REQUESTING it limits the interval so the next send is at most one second past the lease expiry (this clamp is not applied in S_REQUESTING). It chooses the destination: broadcast in S_REQUESTING or S_REBOOTING or after the rebind time, otherwise the server address; the source is the active lease address except in S_REQUESTING and S_REBOOTING (then 0.0.0.0). The seconds field is the saved client->secs in S_REQUESTING and the elapsed interval (capped at 65535) otherwise. It logs, sends the stored request packet with send_packet_unpriv and schedules send_request again at cur_time plus the interval.

Reviewers: original (the expired-lease path returns after S_INIT without sending a packet or scheduling a timeout) right, 1573-1591; round 15 (the interval is not clamped to the lease expiry when the state is S_REQUESTING) right, 1610-1614. Tally 2 right.

name: main
prose: Entry point of dumpon: it configures (or removes) the kernel dump device or a netdump target and does not return. Options: -C cipher, -c client address, -g gateway, -i insert index, -k public key file, -l list, -r remove, -s server, -v verbose, -Z zstd, -z gzip; an unknown option calls usage(). It exits with EX_USAGE (errx) for an unrecognised cipher, for -C when built without crypto, for -i outside 0 to KDA_APPEND-2, for -z together with -Z, for -i together with -r, and, with crypto, for -C given without a public key file; a failed OpenSSL initialisation (when -k is given) exits with EX_UNAVAILABLE, as does -k when built without crypto. With -l it calls listdumpdev() and exits EX_OK. Without -l it requires exactly one operand (usage() otherwise). If both server and client are given the device is the netdump device and the operand is the interface name; if neither is given the operand is the dump device ("off" means remove with /dev/null, and for /dev/null any netdump configuration is first removed through an ioctl, exiting with 1 on failure); any other combination calls usage(). It opens the device with opendumpdev, checks its size unless netdump, compression or removal is in use, and fills the kernel-dump request (remove or insert index, compression zstd, gzip or none). For netdump it resolves the server with getaddrinfo (exit EX_OSERR or EX_NOHOST on failure), copies the interface name and parses the server, client and gateway addresses (the gateway is looked up or defaults to the server), exiting with EX_USAGE for an invalid interface name or address. With a public key it generates the encryption key with genkey. It issues DIOCSKERNELDUMP, retries without compression when it fails with EINVAL and -z or -Z was given (with a warning if the retry succeeds), checks the link status after a netdump success, wipes and frees the key material, and on a final failure exits with EX_OSERR (with a specific message for ENODEV on netdump). On success it lists the dump devices when -v was given and exits with EX_OK.

name: write_s0
prose: Writes the in-memory MBR (mboot.bootinst with its partition table) to the disk and returns 0 or -1. If the global iotest is set it only prints the table with print_s0 and returns 0 without writing. Otherwise it encodes the NDOSPART partition entries from mboot.parts into mboot.bootinst at DOSPARTOFF, stores the DOS magic (DOSMAGIC, little-endian) at DOSMAGICOFFSET, and calls write_disk for each of mboot.bootinst_size / secsize sectors. It returns -1 after a warning if write_disk returns -1, but write_disk (fdisk.c:794-812) returns only 0 on success and EINVAL on a failed or short pwrite (after printing a warning), never -1, so in practice a failed write is not detected here: the loop continues and the function returns 0 at the end.

Reviewer round 15 (formal contract requires only \true, omitting the buffer and secsize preconditions and side effects) right, contract removed. Old prose substantially matches; reworded to avoid "always returns 0" since the -1 branch exists but cannot be taken. Tally 1 right.

name: checkfstab
prose: Checks the filesystems listed in /etc/fstab by pass number: docheck decides whether an entry is checked and checkit checks one filesystem; flags is a mix of CHECK_PREEN, CHECK_DEBUG, CHECK_VERBOSE and DO_BACKGRD. It returns 8 if the checklist cannot be opened (setfsent fails). For each pass (starting at 1 and following the next higher fs_passno) it scans the fstab entries of that pass that docheck accepts. When CHECK_PREEN is clear, or the pass is 1, or DO_BACKGRD is set, each entry is checked synchronously with checkit and a non-zero result is returned immediately; an entry without a device name returns 8 in preen mode and is skipped otherwise. In preen mode in later passes an entry without a device name prints "BAD DISK NAME" and ORs 8 into the status, and other entries are queued per disk (with the failok option). After such a pass it starts the per-disk checks with startdisk (returning its non-zero error code immediately) and waits for the children: for each child that exited normally the exit status is used, except that it is 0 for entries with failok (with a message), and a child killed by a signal counts as 8; a failed entry is kept in the bad list and its status is ORed into the sum, a good one is freed, and the next partition of that disk is started (startdisk error returned immediately). After all passes: if CHECK_PREEN is clear it returns 0; if the accumulated status is non-zero it prints the list of failed filesystems (when there is one) and returns the status; otherwise it calls endfsent and returns 0.

Reviewers: original (non-preen mode and pass 1 call checkit synchronously rather than spawning children) right, 117-130; round 15 (a synchronous checkit failure returns non-zero even when CHECK_PREEN is clear) right, 127-128. Tally 2 right.

name: allocdir
prose: Allocates a new directory inode for fsck_ffs, creates its first block with "." and ".." entries, links it under parent, and returns the new inode number or 0 on failure. The arguments are the parent inode number, the requested inode number (0 for any, as accepted by allocino) and the permission bits mode, which are combined with IFDIR. It returns 0 if allocino returns 0. Otherwise it fills the shared directory template with ino as "." and parent as "..", reads the inode's first block with getdirblk; if that buffer has errors (b_errs non-zero) it calls freeino(ino) and irelse and returns 0. It copies the template into the block, fills the rest of the fragment with empty directory chunks, marks the buffer dirty, sets the inode's link count to 2 and marks the inode dirty. For the root inode (UFS_ROOTINO) it caches the inode info with parent as parent and dotdot, marks it new, sets its type to DT_DIR and its link count, releases the inode and returns ino without checking the parent. For any other inode it first checks INO_IS_DVALID(parent); if the parent is not a valid directory it calls freeino(ino), releases the inode and returns 0. Otherwise it caches the inode info, records the parent, depth (parent's depth plus one, stored in the inode) when the parent's info is found (an unknown parent calls pfatal("allocdir: UNKNOWN PARENT DIR") and continues), sets the type DT_DIR, copies the parent's state, and when that state is DSTATE sets the new inode's link count and increments the parent's link count in the tables. It then increments the parent inode's on-disk link count (for "..") and returns ino. The directory block buffer obtained from getdirblk is not released inside this function.

name: checkfilesys
prose: Checks one filesystem (filesys, a device or mount point) with fsck_ffs and returns a status or exits. It initialises the fsck state, resolves the device (the mount source or blockcheck), opens it and reads the superblock (a failure sets sbreadfailed). In background-check mode (bkgrdcheck) it exits 3 if the superblock cannot be read, 4 if the filesystem is flagged as needing fsck or the journal check passes, 5 if soft updates are not in use, 6 if the kernel lacks the adjrefcnt sysctl, 7 if the filesystem is clean, and otherwise 0. With ckclean and skipclean it again exits 3 on a superblock read failure, may open the device for writing, and for a gjournal filesystem exits 0 if it is clean or runs gjournal_check and exits 0 or 4. With bkgrdflag it calls setup_bkgrdchk: -1 goes to the clean report (prints the free counts and returns 0), 0 exits with EEXIT, 1 sets preen and continues. It then calls setup(filesys): 0 prints "CAN'T CHECK FILE SYSTEM" (in preen mode) and returns EEXIT, -1 prints the clean report and returns 0. For a journaled (SUJ) filesystem it may run suj_check and exit 0 or 4. It may offer to add check-hash protection when not preening and not -y, then runs pass1, pass1b when there are duplicates, pass2, pass3, pass4 and pass5 (pass5 is skipped, with a message, when a cylinder group header is corrupt), prints the statistics, cleans up and calls ckfini(resolved). It then returns ERESTART if a rerun is needed, a restart is wanted and fewer than 10 restarts happened and (preen or the user answers yes); otherwise, if chkdoreload reports a reload it returns 0 when the filesystem was not modified and else syncs and returns 4; the last result is ERERUN if rerun is set and 0 otherwise.

name: pass2
prose: Phase 2 of fsck_ffs (check directory connectivity); it takes no arguments, returns nothing, and relies on pass 1 having filled the inoinfo table and the sorted array inpsort of directories. It first examines the root inode state: unallocated (USTATE) asks to ALLOCATE and calls allocdir; a cleared one asks to REALLOCATE (freedirino then allocdir) or CONTINUE; a non-directory root asks to REALLOCATE or FIX (changing the mode to a directory); a directory state is left; any other state calls errx(EEXIT). If the user declines to allocate or continue it calls ckfini(0) and exit(EEXIT); a failed allocdir calls errx(EEXIT, "CANNOT ALLOCATE ROOT INODE"). It then marks the root DFOUND and the whiteout inode FSTATE (type DT_WHT), sorts inpsort by block with blksort, and for each directory with non-zero size reports progress on signals, fixes a size below MINDIRSIZE (after reply("FIX") for the on-disk size) or not a multiple of DIRBLKSIZ (adjusting it in preen mode or after reply("ADJUST")), builds a temporary directory dinode from the recorded blocks and runs ckinode with pass2check on it. In a second loop, for each directory with a non-zero parent and size: a directory whose parent is DFOUND and which is still unfound becomes DFOUND; when i_dotdot equals i_parent or is (ino_t)-1 nothing more is done; when i_dotdot is 0 it creates the missing ".." entry automatically with makeentry and decrements the parent's link count (no user prompt); otherwise it reports the bad ".." entry and, in snapshot mode, fixes it with the vfs.ffs.setcwd and setdotdot sysctls (on a failure it only prints and skips), or in normal mode fixes it after preen or reply("FIX") with link count adjustments and changeino (a declined fix leaves the entry unchanged). Finally it calls propagate(). The function does not return a status.

Reviewers: original ('..' pointers may stay inconsistent when the user declines FIX or the snapshot setdotdot fails; skipped directories too) right, 261-264 and 246-254; round 15 (automatic i_dotdot == 0 makeentry rewrite adjusts the link count without user acceptance; zero-parent directories are still scanned in the first loop) right, 212-219 and 137-151. Tally 2 right.

name: pass2check
prose: Callback run by ckinode for each directory entry of a directory being checked in pass 2; it returns KEEPON, ORed with ALTERED when it changed the entry buffer, and never returns any other value (a bad inode state calls errx(EEXIT)). idesc->id_dirp is the current entry, id_number the directory inode and id_entryno the position. For entry 0 it checks that the entry is "." with the directory's own inode number and type DT_DIR, fixing them when reply("FIX") agrees, and otherwise offers to add or replace it with "." (either replacing the whole entry or splitting off space), which can be declined, leaving "." missing. For entries 0 and 1 it checks the ".." entry in the same way: an out-of-range inode number is replaced by the recorded parent (or the root) after reply("FIX"), the type is corrected, i_dotdot is set from the entry; a missing ".." is added or replaced after reply, and if the user declines i_dotdot is set to (ino_t)-1; link counts are adjusted when a new entry splits an existing one (the link count of an existing entry's inode is decremented without a range check at lines 360 and 437). A free entry (inode 0) returns KEEPON. Later entries named "." or ".." (entry number 2 or higher) are cleared after reply("FIX"). For other entries it clears them if the inode number is out of range or the user answers REMOVE for an unallocated or cleared inode, fixes whiteout/type mismatches, propagates the DFOUND state from the directory to subdirectories, sets i_parent of a directory's first-found parent (calling fix_extraneous for a directory named a second time, which can ask to remove the entry), corrects the entry type and decrements the inode's link count. If the entry is to be removed it sets d_ino to 0 and returns ret | KEEPON | ALTERED; otherwise ret | KEEPON.

Reviewers: original (the function always returns KEEPON possibly with ALTERED and may leave '.' missing when the user declines) right, 325-326 and 573-576; round 15 (inoinfo(dirp->d_ino) is used before any range check in the '..' handling, so the old precondition is wrong) right, 360 and 437 versus 466. name: fix_extraneous
prose: Called from pass2check when a directory inp already has a recorded parent and another directory entry (idesc, in directory idesc->id_number) also names it. It returns 1 to tell the caller to clear the new entry, or 0. If inp->i_dotdot is 0 it first looks up ".." in the directory named by the new entry with ckinode/findino and records it in i_dotdot when found. In cases 1 to 4 (i_dotdot is 0, or the new entry is in the recorded parent, or i_dotdot differs from the entry's directory, or i_dotdot equals the recorded parent) it prints the extraneous-link message and: in a snapshot (cursnapshot non-zero) removes the new name with the vfs.ffs.setcwd and vfs.ffs.unlink sysctls (reporting a failure) and returns 0 in all sub-cases; otherwise returns 1 in preen mode, and the answer of reply("REMOVE") otherwise. In case 5 (the new entry's directory is the one ".." points to), it prints the message and: in a snapshot removes the old name with the sysctls (a failing sysctl returns 0 without changing anything) and sets inp->i_parent to the new directory without touching the link count, returning 0; otherwise, if not preening and the user declines it returns 0, else it deletes the old entry from the old parent with ckinode and deleteentry, sets i_parent to idesc->id_number, increments the link count of inp's inode in inoinfo and returns 0.

Reviewers: original (returning 0 in cases 1-4 removes the new name without reparenting) right for the snapshot path, 630-651; round 15 (the case 5 snapshot path sets i_parent but does not increment ino_linkcnt; the old prose said both happen) right, 692-693 vs 706-707. name: main
prose: Entry point of ggatel (GEOM Gate local provider tool); it does not return. The action comes from argv[1] (create, rescue, destroy or list, case-insensitive); a missing or unknown action calls usage(). Options are parsed with getopt "fo:s:t:u:v": -f (force) only for destroy, -o ro, wo, rw or direct only for create and rescue (any other value is errx(EXIT_FAILURE)), -s sectorsize and -t timeout only for create, -u unit for all, -v verbose except for destroy; an option not allowed for the action calls usage(). The -s, -t and -u values are converted with strtoul/strtol and rejected only when the result is 0 and errno is non-zero, so a non-numeric argument that converts to 0 with errno 0 is accepted as 0. After the options it requires, per action: create needs exactly one operand (the path), loads the module, opens the control device and calls g_gatel_create(); rescue needs one operand and a unit (otherwise "Required unit number." and usage()), opens the device and calls g_gatel_rescue(); destroy needs a unit (same message), sets verbose and calls g_gate_destroy(unit, force) after opening the device; list calls g_gate_list(unit, verbose). Any other state calls usage(). Afterwards it closes the control device with g_gate_close_device() and exits with EXIT_SUCCESS (g_gatel_create and rescue may not return, not read).

name: main
prose: Entry point of growfs, which enlarges a UFS filesystem; it returns 0 at the end or exits through err/errx. Options: -N (dry run), -s size (parsed with strtoumax base 0 and scaled: a bare number by DEV_BSIZE, b/B by 1, k/K, m/M, g/G and t/T by powers of 1024; any other suffix is errx(2)), -v (ignored) and -y; an unknown option calls usage(), as does an operand count other than one. It resolves the device with getmntpoint/getdev (errx(2) if it cannot be found), opens it read-only (err(3)), reads the media size (err(3) on failure, errx(2) if below 1) and the superblock with sbget (errx(2) for an unrecognised superblock, errc(3) for a read error), and exits 2 if the filesystem is flagged unclean or needing fsck. The target size is the media size when -s is absent, otherwise the -s value (errx(2) if larger than the media), rounded down to the fragment size. If it is not larger than the current size it exits with errx(0) for equal and errx(2) for smaller. It computes the new superblock size; if the old size is not below the new one it calls errx(3, "we are not growing"). Unless -y it errors out (errx(2)) if active snapshots exist, and unless -y or -N it prints the warning and asks for confirmation (any reply other than "yes" exits 0). Unless -N it suspends a mounted read-write filesystem through the ufssuspend device (err(3) on failure) or opens the device for writing (err(3)); it reads and rewrites the last fragment as a write test, recomputes the cylinder group count (dropping a last group too small to use and exiting errx(3) with "not enough new space" if there is no growth), calls growfs(), closes the descriptors, resumes the filesystem with UFSRESUME and closes the output (err(3) on failure), and for a read-only mount calls chkdoreload and exits 9 if it fails. It then returns 0.

name: ctrl_thread
prose: Thread function of the HAST worker that serves the control connection res->hr_ctrl; arg is the struct hast_resource. It loops forever and returns only by pthread_exit. Each iteration receives a header nvlist with hast_proto_recv_hdr; if that fails it calls pthread_exit(NULL) immediately when sigexit_received is set, and otherwise logs an error, sends SIGTERM to its own process and calls pthread_exit(NULL). It reads the "cmd" field; a message without cmd (value 0) logs an error, frees the message and continues without sending a reply. For the status command it builds a reply with "complete" or "degraded" depending on whether both remote connections exist, the extent size, keepdirty and dirty counts (non-zero only for the primary role) and the statistics counters, calls the resource's output_status_aux, and sets "error" to 0; for the reload command (which asserts the primary role) it calls primary_config_reload and sets "error" to 0; any other command sets "error" to EINVAL. It frees the incoming message; if building the reply failed (nv_error) it logs an error, frees the reply and continues without replying; otherwise it sends the reply with hast_proto_send (a send failure is only logged) and frees it.

name: compression_recv
prose: Decompresses a received HAST data buffer according to the "compression" field of the nvlist nv; the parameters are the resource (unused), the nvlist, the buffer pointer *datap, its size *sizep and the flag *freedatap saying whether *datap is heap-owned. If nv has no "compression" string it returns 0 without changing anything. If the algorithm is "hole" it calls hast_hole_decompress, if "lzf" hast_lzf_decompress, each with the current buffer and a local copy of the size; any other name logs "Unknown compression algorithm" and returns -1 without changing anything. If the decompressor returns NULL it returns -1 leaving *datap, *sizep and *freedatap unchanged. Otherwise it frees the old buffer only when *freedatap was true, sets *freedatap to true, stores the new buffer in *datap, the decompressed size in *sizep and returns 0.

name: main_loop
prose: Main event loop of the hastd parent process; it takes no arguments and does not return. Each iteration calls check_signals(), builds a read set containing the control connection descriptor, every non-NULL listen connection, every resource's event connection and, for resources in the primary role, their hr_conn (asserting the descriptors are valid and fit FD_SETSIZE), and calls select with a REPORT_INTERVAL timeout. After select it calls hook_check() and updates lastcheck when REPORT_INTERVAL seconds have passed since the last check. If select returned 0 or failed with EINTR it starts the next iteration; for any other select error it removes the pid file and calls pjdlog_exit(EX_OSERR). Otherwise it calls check_signals() again, then handles the ready descriptors: control_handle(cfg) for the control connection, listen_accept for each ready listen connection, and for each resource with an event connection: if the event descriptor is ready, event_recv is called and, when it returns 0, the loop goes to the next resource (so the resource's hr_conn is not examined in this iteration), otherwise the event connection and the resource's hr_conn are closed and set to NULL; if the event descriptor is not ready and the role is primary, connection_migrate(res) is called when hr_conn is ready.

name: listen_accept
prose: Accepts one incoming connection on listen entry lst and handles the HAST handshake; it returns nothing. It accepts the connection with proto_accept (on failure it returns), gets the local and remote addresses, sets the protocol timeout, and finds a resource whose configured remote address matches the connecting address (closing the connection if there is none). It receives the handshake header (close on failure) and reads the "resource" name (missing: close), "version" (0 is treated as 1) and the optional "token" (a token of the wrong size closes the connection). It then looks up the resource by name; each of the following failures builds an error message nvlist and goes to fail, which sends it back and closes the connection: unknown resource ("Resource not configured."), address no longer matching ("No access to the resource."), a role other than secondary (with a "wait" flag if the local role is primary), and a token that does not match the stored token. Without a token (the first connection): an existing worker process is signalled with SIGINT, waited for and cleaned up (failures logged), or an existing half-open incoming connection is closed and dropped; the version is capped at HAST_PROTO_VERSION and stored in res->hr_version, a fresh random token is generated into res->hr_token, a reply with the version and token is built and sent (a build or send failure goes to fail), and the connection is stored in res->hr_remotein. With a token (the second connection) the connection is stored in res->hr_remoteout and hastd_secondary(res, nvin) is called (which takes the handshake further). On success it frees the nvlists and clears the log prefix without closing the connection (it now belongs to the resource); on fail or close it frees the nvlists, closes the connection and clears the prefix.

name: remote_recv_thread
prose: Thread of the HAST primary that receives replies from the secondary for component 1 (ncomp = 1); arg is the hast_resource; it loops forever and returns NULL only syntactically. Each iteration waits on hio_recv_list_cond until the receive list is non-empty. If the remote component is not connected (ISCONNECTED false) it removes the first request, sets hio_errors[1] to ENOTCONN and moves it to the done path (goto done_queue). Otherwise it receives the reply header; on failure it logs, closes the remote connection with remote_close and goes to the next iteration. A reply without "seq", or one whose seq matches no request on the receive list (the matching request is removed from the list), frees the nvlist and continues. A reply with a non-zero "error" sets that error in hio_errors[1], logs a warning and goes to the done path. For a BIO_READ it takes the remote lock, goes to the done path without setting hio_errors[1] if the connection is gone, and receives the data with hast_proto_recv_data; a receive failure stores errno in hio_errors[1], closes the connection and goes to the done path (not continue). Other commands carry no data; an unknown command aborts. On success hio_errors[1] is set to 0. For a memsync write the first (memsync) acknowledgment releases hio_writecount, calls write_complete when it reaches zero and hio_errors[0] is 0, marks the request as memsync-acknowledged and, if there was no error, puts the request back at the tail of the receive list and continues to wait for the final reply. Finally it releases hio_countdown; if other references remain it continues, otherwise a sync request (ISSYNCREQ) is completed with SYNCREQDONE under sync_lock and signals sync_cond, and any other request is moved to the done queue.

name: yygetc
prose: Returns the next character for the ipf configuration lexer, from the lookahead buffer yytext or from the current source, using the globals yypos, yylast, yylineNum, pos, string_start/string_end/string_val and yyin; docont non-zero enables backslash-newline continuation. If yypos < yylast it returns yytext[yypos], increments yypos, increments yylineNum if the character is '\n', and leaves yylast unchanged. Otherwise, if yypos == YYBUFSIZ it returns TOOLONG without changing anything. Otherwise it takes the character from string_val[pos - string_start] when pos lies in [string_start, string_end] (incrementing yypos once at that point) or else reads it with fgetc(yyin); for the stream case with docont set, a backslash makes it read the next character and, if that is a newline, count the line and read one more. It increments yylineNum if the character is '\n', stores it at yytext[yypos] and increments yypos again (so in the string_val branch yypos ends two above its old value and the character is stored one slot past the old yypos), sets yylast to yypos, NUL-terminates yytext at yypos and returns the character.

name: bpf_validate
prose: Checks that the BPF program f of len instructions is well formed and returns 1 if it is and 0 otherwise. It returns 1 immediately for len == 0 (without reading f), and 0 for len < 1 after that or len > BPF_MAXINSNS. For each instruction it switches on the class: for load classes the mode must be one of the accepted immediate, absolute, indirect, MSH and length modes, with the scratch-memory mode requiring k < BPF_MEMWORDS and any other mode returning 0; for store classes k must be < BPF_MEMWORDS; for ALU instructions the operation must be a known one, and a division or modulus by the constant 0 returns 0; for jumps the operation must be a known one: an unconditional jump needs from + k not to overflow and to stay below len (from = i + 1), conditional jumps need from + jt and from + jf below len; return, misc classes are accepted; any unknown class returns 0. After the loop it returns 1 only if the class of the last instruction f[len - 1] is BPF_RET. It does not modify f.

name: emitGroup
prose: Part of the ipf rule compiler: it emits C source text for one rule or for the closing of a rule group to the output file; the parameters are the rule number num (negative values mean end-of-group markers, -2 emitting the rule-pointer arrays), the direction dir (0 in, 1 out, -1 none), v (an array of FRC_MAX mc_t records), the rule fr, the group name and the in/out rule counts. It keeps static state: fp (set from cfile when unset; it returns immediately if both are NULL), the saved group name egroup, openfunc, the saved comparison array n, the nesting depth sin and the per-direction header flags. When the group differs from the saved one it prints closing braces for the open nesting levels (sin - 1 down to 1), and if a function is open (openfunc == 1) it prints "return (fr);" and the closing brace, clears openfunc and frees n; it then resets sin and the header flags and saves the new group name. When the group is the same, a function is open and num < 0, it frees n, prints the closing braces and, if still open, the return and brace and clears openfunc. dir == -1 returns here. It finds the matching group in the groups list for the direction; for num == -2 with dir 0 or 1 and header[0] unset and non-zero counts it prints the ipf_rules_in_ or ipf_rules_out_ pointer array (the out case also sets fp to NULL); any num below 0 then returns. For a rule it prints the function header for the group and direction the first time (openfunc = 1, with src/dst variables when needed), marks which of the FRC_MAX comparisons apply from the rule, sorts them, computes the indentation shared with the previous rule's comparisons (closing braces for the levels that end), prints the nested if-tests for the comparisons, prints either a return of the rule (for quick rules) or an assignment to fr, copies the comparison array into n (allocating it if needed) and stores the new depth in sin.

name: main
prose: Entry point of ipfstat, which displays IPFilter statistics, rules, states or authentication information; it returns 0 after the display, or exits earlier. It first scans the options once (without error reporting) only for -M (memory file) and -N (kernel image), which set live_kernel to 0. For a live kernel it opens the state, auth, NAT and filter devices (perror and exit(-1) if one fails); when -M or -N was given it drops setuid/setgid privileges; for a live kernel it checks the device revision, otherwise it opens the kernel image with openkmem (exit(-1) on failure); it then drops privileges again. It parses the options a second time: -4/-6 (when built with IPv6), -a, -A, -C, -d, -D, -f, -g, -h, -i, -I, -l, -m (an invalid ipf expression exits 1), -n, -o, -O, -P (an unknown protocol exits -2), -R, -s, -S, -t (exits -2 if STATETOP is not built in), -T (a refresh time below 1 exits -2) and -v; an unknown option calls usage(). With IPv6 support, -4 or -6 without -i, -o or -t exits -2, and without either both families are selected. It then reads the statistics with ipfstate_live (zeroing the structures first) or ipfstate_dead. It selects the display by an if/else chain: states (-s) shows the IP states and nothing else; a list option calls showlist and, when both -i and -o are set, clears the output flag and calls showlist a second time; otherwise the frag states (-f), the state-top display (-t, when built in), authentication statistics (-A), groups (-g), or by default the general statistics. It returns 0.
